The story is the legend, the inequality is a constraint, and the worked days are the note.

feedback.correct: Each part answers one question: what, in what shape, how big, and an example.

byKey.t-cons: The inequality is a constraint. The input format says only what comes in which order.
byKey.t-note: That sentence explains the example's answer, so it is the note.
byKey.t-legend: The story about Mira is the legend. It sets the scene but promises nothing about the tests.

explain.text: The judge checks only the formats and the constraints. The legend is decoration that may mislead; the examples and the note are there to check your reading. So we read the constraints first, then the output, then the legend.

Each test case has two lines: n, then
The sum of n over all test cases does not
params.title: Problem A, many test cases

screens.question: At most how many P&L values can one whole input contain?

widget.label: Values in one input
widget.accept: 200,000: the sum of $n$ over all test cases is at most $2 \cdot 10^5$.

hints.text: Which line bounds all the test cases together?
The last sentence bounds the total.
However the values are split into tests, they add up to at most $2 \cdot 10^5$.

feedback.correct: At most 200,000 values in total, however they are split.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the sentence about the sum of $n$.

byKey.product: You multiplied $t$ by the largest $n$. The sum bound stops every test being that large at once.
byKey.tests: $10^4$ is the most test cases. Each holds at least one value, and the total is bounded separately.

explain.text: The sum bound means the whole input is as big as one large test. Work that is linear in each test is linear overall. Without the bound, $10^4$ tests of $2 \cdot 10^5$ values would be $2 \cdot 10^9$ numbers.

screens.title: Does the answer fit?
screens.prose: Problem C asks for Mira's total P&L over all $n$ days: the sum of the $a_i$. The constraints are the same as A's. In C++, an `int` holds up to 2,147,483,647, about $2.1 \cdot 10^9$.
screens.question: Which C++ type should hold the total?

options.why: Each value fits, but $2 \cdot 10^5$ values of $10^9$ add to $2 \cdot 10^{14}$.
It reaches only about $4.3 \cdot 10^9$, and it cannot hold a loss.

hints.text: Multiply the largest $n$ by the largest $|a_i|$.
That is far above $2.1 \cdot 10^9$, so the sum needs 64 bits: `long long`, up to about $9.2 \cdot 10^{18}$.

feedback.correct: $2 \cdot 10^{14}$ needs 64 bits. In Python the integer simply grows.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Bound the total, not one value.

byKey.int: You checked one value. The total of $2 \cdot 10^5$ of them can reach $2 \cdot 10^{14}$.

explain.text: You bounded the answer by $n \cdot \max|a_i| = 2 \cdot 10^{14}$. A C++ `int` would overflow without any error and print a wrong number. Python's integers have no fixed width, so the same code is safe there.

screens.title: Read many tests
screens.prose: Write `parse(text)`. It takes a whole input in the many-test format above, as one string. It returns `(t, cases)`, where `cases` is a list of $t$ lists of ints. Real inputs may lack a final newline or carry blank lines.

lines: The first line contains t (1 ≤ t ≤ 10⁴),
Each test case has two lines: n, then
The sum of n over all test cases does not
params.title: Problem A, many test cases

screens.question: Write `parse(text)`.

widget.solution:
def parse(text):
    tokens = text.split()
    t = int(tokens[0])
    pos = 1
    cases = []
    for _ in range(t):
        n = int(tokens[pos])
        pos += 1
        cases.append([int(x) for x in tokens[pos:pos + n]])
        pos += n
    return t, cases

tests.call: (lambda r: (r[0], len(r[1]), sum(len(c) for c in r[1]), r[1][-1]))(parse(text))

widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests. Test 2 has no final newline. Tests 3 and 4 have blank lines at the end and between test cases. Test 7 has $t = 10^4$ test cases of 20 values each.

hints.text: Splitting on whitespace ignores line breaks and blank lines alike.
`text.split()` gives every number as a token, in order.
Read `t`, then for each test read `n` and the next `n` tokens, moving a position `pos` forward.

feedback.correct: One split, then a position that walks through the tokens.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the first failing test's input.

byKey.test-2: Test 2 has no newline at the end. Reading by lines may lose or break the last line.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 ends with blank lines. `text.split()` ignores them; `text.split('\n')` does not.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 has blank lines between test cases. Read tokens, not lines.
byKey.test-7: Test 7 is large. `tokens.pop(0)` shifts the whole list on every call; move an index instead.

explain.text: `text.split()` turns the input into tokens, whatever the line breaks. A position `pos` then reads $n$ and the next $n$ values, test by test. The whole parse is $O(\text{input size})$.

screens.title: An online assessment
screens.prose: Trading firms often screen developers with an online assessment: two or three statements like this, auto-graded, against a clock. Five minutes of reading saves twenty of debugging.

ticker, a side (B or S) and a quantity.
For each ticker that traded, print its net
position, in the order the tickers first
params.title: Online assessment, question 1

Per ticker, sorted by name: sum $+q$ for B and $-q$ for S

quiz.prose: A statement says: $1 \le t \le 10^4$, $n \ge 1$ in every test case, and the sum of $n$ over all test cases does not exceed $3 \cdot 10^5$.
quiz.question: With $t = 10^4$ test cases, what is the largest $n$ one test case can have?

widget.label: Largest single n
widget.accept: 290,001: the other 9,999 tests hold at least one value each.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Every other test case needs at least one value.

byKey.all: You gave one test the whole sum. The other 9,999 tests each need $n \ge 1$.
byKey.even: That is the average. The question asks how large one test can be.

explain.text: The sum bound is shared. With $t = 10^4$, the other 9,999 tests take at least 9,999 values, leaving $300{,}000 - 9{,}999 = 290{,}001$.

quiz.prose: A statement has $n \le 10^5$ and $1 \le a_i \le 10^6$, and asks for the largest product $a_i \cdot a_j$ with $i \ne j$.
quiz.question: Which C++ type holds the answer?

options.why: Each $a_i$ fits, but a product can reach $10^{12}$, beyond $2.1 \cdot 10^9$.

options.text: Neither: it needs a big-number type
options.why: $10^{12}$ is far below `long long`'s limit of about $9.2 \cdot 10^{18}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Bound the answer, not one input value.

explain.text: The answer is at most $10^6 \cdot 10^6 = 10^{12}$. That overflows an `int` but fits easily in a `long long`. In C++ the multiplication itself must happen in 64 bits: `1LL * a[i] * a[j]`.

quiz.prose: A variant of problem A counts the days whose P&L is **at least** every earlier day's. Day 1 still counts. The test is `2 2 1 3`.
quiz.question: What should the variant print?

feedback.correct: Days 1, 2 and 4: the tie on day 2 counts now.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. *At least* lets a tie count.

byKey.strict: You used the original strict rule. *At least* lets day 2's tie count.
byKey.all: Day 3's 1 is below 2, so it does not count.

explain.text: One word changes the answer from 2 to 3. That is why we restate the task in our own words before coding, with *strictly* or *at least* written in.
